China’s leadership in research and development and in translating energy innovations to commercialization, in part due to its control over supply chains and access to critical minerals and its established and interconnected manufacturing infrastructure, positions the country as the United States’ primary competition for innovative energy technologies. For example, China plans to develop radio frequency power-beaming capabilities in space to capture and transmit solar energy from orbiting PV stations to the ground, unlocking power that is less variable than ground-based solar (Tong 2025). China also has several ocean energy installations along its coast, despite the limited coastal energy available for exploitation, and wave power installations are currently undergoing sea trials (Qing 2023). The South China Sea, particularly the waters surrounding Taiwan, holds significant tidal current energy potential (Wan, Feng, and Zhang 2023). If China is first to deploy marine and hydrokinetic energy at scale, this advancement could strengthen the country’s control over critical maritime areas, such as the South China Sea (and subsequently its control over ports and supply routes), enhance its surveillance capabilities, and potentially disrupt the activities of other nations. Front-runner status in distributed large-scale tidal power assets could translate to advantages in maritime areas with high tidal and wave capacity outside the Indo-Pacific, such as the Persian Gulf, the Black Sea, the Gulf of Oman, the Bay of Biscay, and the French Atlantic. 15 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. DOW investments in promising emerging technologies will be key to maintaining a competitive position on the battlefield. 4.3 Faster Adoption Abroad Broader adoption of advanced energy technologies abroad could hamper the availability of DOW-compatible legacy fuel infrastructure (e.g., gas stations being widely replaced by EV charging stations) or capacity (e.g., aviation fuel tank reserves being replaced by 100% biofuel reserves) during deployments in friendly or hostile destinations. One study estimates that the number of gas stations in Europe will decrease by 45% by 2050 (Consultancy.eu 2024). Some interviewees suggested that a reduction in petroleum-based refueling infrastructure across Europe could impede a land force’s ability to rapidly respond to conflict. Adjusting acquisitions to regional conditions or increasing owned energy provisions could reduce this risk. Faster adoption could also result in the establishment of infrastructure or standards that DOW must adapt to, rather than hold a leading role in choosing the best fit for DOW purposes, and U.S. military concerns, such as cyber or other vulnerabilities, might not be prioritized. For example, the rapid development of offshore wind plants could lead to unforeseen radar interference affecting military or civilian maritime operations nearby (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine 2022), despite permitting processes intended to prevent such impacts. Moreover, the rapid proliferation of offshore wind plants or solar installations in key geopolitical regions could lead to unintended security risks if critical technologies are sourced from countries with competing interests to the United States or those that have less rigorous cybersecurity standards.
